title: Dual-damascene fusion of storage-node contact and landing pad
idea: Combine BEOL dual-damascene with the DRAM buried-contact module: the storage-node contact hole and the landing-pad trench are etched into one stacked dielectric in a single trench-first/via-last sequence, then filled with one Ru or Mo deposition and planarized with one CMP.
why: Removes one critical EUV/SAQP patterning layer, one metal fill and one CMP from the 5-7 EUV-layer flow (fact 4), ~3-5% wafer cost; the Ru/Mo fill also cuts tungsten (China ~80%) exposure.

title: Nanoimprint guide plus block-copolymer multiplication for EUV-free capacitor holes
idea: Combine J-FIL-style nanoimprint, which prints a 4x-relaxed hexagonal guide pattern, with high-chi block-copolymer self-assembly that subdivides each guide cell into a 12 nm-scale honeycomb. The densest DRAM layer, the capacitor holes, then needs no EUV and no SAQP.
why: Takes the capacitor-hole layer off EUV: an NIL tool costs ~$30-40M against ~$200M for EUV, roughly halving litho cost for that layer and easing the single-supplier chokepoint (fact 4).

title: Mature U.S. foundry periphery wafers hybrid-bonded under array-only wafers
idea: Combine Xtacking-style wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with idle U.S. 28-40 nm logic foundry capacity. The DRAM wafer carries only cells, bitline sense amps and wordline drivers; decoders, I/O, DLL, charge pumps and test logic are made on mature logic wafers and bonded face-to-face at ~1 um pitch.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7). The array wafer becomes nearly all cells and drops ~8-12 HKMG periphery masks, and depreciated U.S. fabs supply half the silicon, so array-fab wafer starts per bit fall ~25-35%.

title: Backside-power flow repurposed to build capacitors behind the transistors
idea: Combine backside-power-delivery/BSI wafer thinning with the 1T1C cell: access transistors and bitlines are built on the front, the wafer is bonded to a carrier and thinned to the channel bottoms, and the storage capacitors are formed on the exposed backside drains, so bitline and capacitor no longer compete for one plane.
why: Decouples capacitor thermal budget and geometry from bitline routing, enabling a 4F2 cell at relaxed F (~15 nm rather than 12 nm) and removing ~2 EUV-critical self-aligned contact steps; ~30% density at the same litho (facts 1, 4).

title: Gen-8.5 LCD lines plus panel nanoimprint for oxide gain-cell tiles
idea: Combine written-off display-TFT fabs (oxide sputter and 2.2x2.5 m glass handling) with panel-scale nanoimprint at ~200 nm rules, and build 2T0C oxide gain-cell tiles on glass. The tiles are diced and bonded as a slow capacity tier (~50-100 ns) for cold KV-cache and embeddings.
why: Panel area costs 50-100x less per cm2 than 300 mm wafer area and needs no new capex, no EUV and no HPQ crucibles. Even at ~1 um2 cells, it adds bit supply outside the wafer-fab bottleneck (capital intensity, scarce resources).

title: Shadow-evaporation self-alignment places bitline and storage contacts without masks
idea: Combine the angled shadow deposition used for Dolan-bridge qubit junctions with the 6F2 cell. The buried-wordline trench topography acts as a built-in stencil, and two directional depositions at +theta and -theta drop the bitline-contact and storage-contact metals on opposite sides of each active pillar.
why: Eliminates 1-2 contact-defining masks and their overlay budget (fact 4); contacts are self-aligned by geometry, giving ~5% cost reduction plus yield gain.

title: Maskless multi-beam writing for periphery, mask-defined SAQP for array
idea: Combine 260k-beamlet e-beam writers, today used only to make masks, with the DRAM product flow. Irregular, sparse periphery layers that change with every product are direct-written with no reticle, while the regular array uses one shared immersion-SAQP mask set.
why: Removes ~10-15 periphery reticles per product (a $10-20M mask set per design spin). LPDDR, HBM-core and custom AI SKUs can share one array mask set, which lowers the capital barrier for new U.S. entrants.

title: Bosch-etched TSVs and deep-trench storage cells in one etch
idea: Combine MEMS Bosch deep-reactive-ion etching with eDRAM-style deep-trench capacitors on 200 mm MEMS/power fabs. One DRIE step cuts both the stack TSVs and 40 um-deep trench capacitors (Cs >100 fF) for a relaxed-pitch, near-refresh-free buffer DRAM die.
why: Uses abundant, depreciated U.S. 200 mm capacity. Huge Cs cuts refresh ~100x (fact 3), and the TSV step becomes a shared step rather than an added tax (fact 6). Density is low, so this is a buffer/cache tier.

title: Area-selective ALD merges wordline-module patterning and deposition
idea: Combine area-selective ALD (inhibitor monolayers that block growth on SiN/SiO2) with the buried-wordline module. The gate dielectric grows only on exposed trench silicon and the Mo/TiN wordline grows only on that dielectric, so recess, cap and isolation self-align without block masks.
why: Cuts ~2 masks and ~15 dep/etch/clean steps in the wordline module, ~4% fewer tool-hours per wafer (fact 4).

title: Metal SADP spacers become the finished bitlines
idea: Combine self-aligned double patterning with metallization: the spacer is deposited conformally as Ru or Mo rather than oxide, etched back, and the mandrel removed, so the spacers are the bitlines. Hard-mask transfer, metal deposition, metal etch and two cleans are skipped.
why: Removes ~8-10 steps per bitline layer and avoids stacking line-edge roughness from transfer etches; Ru/Mo also avoid tungsten (process steps, scarce resource).

title: Grayscale multi-tone EUV exposure defines via and line together
idea: Combine grayscale lithography from micro-optics with a dose-to-depth metal-oxide resist. A three-level attenuated reticle gives contacts full dose and lines half dose, so the resist develops a two-depth relief that transfers via plus trench in one etch.
why: Halves EUV exposures for paired via/line levels in the bitline and periphery metals, saving ~$150-250 per wafer per pass avoided (fact 4).

title: Anodic aluminum oxide pores serve as the capacitor mold
idea: Combine electrochemical anodization (self-ordered AAO reaches aspect ratios above 200 in wet baths) with the DRAM capacitor. Al is deposited over the landing pads and imprint-textured so pores nucleate over each pad, anodized at room temperature into 15-20 nm pores 2-3 um deep, and the electrodes and dielectric are then ALD-coated inside.
why: Replaces the most capital-intensive DRAM tool, high-aspect-ratio plasma etch of the 60-75:1 mold, with bath processing. AR ~115 becomes reachable (fact 1) for ~+50% Cs, and module capex falls ~5x.

title: Excimer-laser crystallized silicon tiers for monolithic 3D DRAM
idea: Combine LTPS-display line-beam laser crystallization with 3D DRAM: amorphous Si tiers are deposited one at a time over the finished lower tiers, and each is melted and crystallized by a nanosecond laser that heats only the top ~50 nm. This replaces Si/SiGe epitaxial superlattices.
why: Avoids strain-limited epi superlattices and the selective SiGe removal etch, so tier count is not capped by epitaxy and stays within BEOL thermal budget (fact 2).

title: Convert idle 3D NAND toolsets into vertical-bitline 3D DRAM lines
idea: Combine the 3D NAND toolset (staircase, channel-hole etch, replacement gate) with a vertical-bitline, horizontal-capacitor 3D DRAM whose steps map one-to-one onto NAND tools: the alternating stack becomes Si/SiGe or oxide-semiconductor layers, the channel hole becomes the bitline hole, and gate replacement becomes capacitor replacement.
why: Reuses existing $10-20B NAND fabs instead of 3-5-year, $15B+ greenfield DRAM fabs. NAND tools already handle 200+ layers, far past the ~26-tier break-even (facts 2, 4).

title: Temporary-bond tester wafer probes every die in one touch
idea: Combine temporary direct bonding with wafer probing: a reusable tester wafer carrying BIST controllers and power delivery is bonded face-to-face to the DRAM wafer through the fine-pitch pads later used for stacking. It runs all die tests in parallel and then debonds.
why: Probe cards and ATE are ~10% of DRAM capex. Whole-wafer parallel test cuts tester count and test time ~10x and makes known-good die for HBM cheaper (fact 6).

title: Kerfless porous-silicon lift-off reuses each crystal-grown wafer tenfold
idea: Combine solar-industry epitaxial lift-off (porous-Si release layer under 20 um epitaxy) with DRAM. The memory is built in the epi layer, bonded device-side to a carrier or logic wafer, cleaved at the porous layer, and the CZ parent wafer is re-polished and reused 10+ times.
why: Cuts prime-wafer demand ~10x and with it the Spruce Pine (>80%) high-purity quartz crucible dependence. Wafer cost (~5-8% of DRAM cost) falls, and HBM thinning comes free (scarce resources, fact 6).

title: Liquid-metal membrane chuck replaces helium backside cooling
idea: Combine the electrostatic chuck with a sealed, compliant membrane filled with gallium-indium liquid metal or a phase-change medium that conducts heat from the wafer backside. This removes the helium backside gas used in every etch and deposition chamber.
why: Helium is a chokepoint, with Qatar's ~30% offline since March 2026, and a DRAM fab runs thousands of He-cooled chambers. Removing He dependence also improves temperature uniformity for capacitor etch.

title: FOUPs that pre-clean wafers while traveling between tools
idea: Combine overhead automated transport with a vapor-phase process chamber: smart FOUPs with onboard N2 purge, HF-vapor native-oxide removal and UV dehydration run queue-time-critical pre-clean steps in transit. Time-linked sequences then no longer need dedicated tool clusters.
why: Queue-time constraints idle ~5-10% of DRAM tool capacity and force tool duplication; in-transit processing reclaims it (capital intensity, throughput).

title: Spatial ALD-ALE supercycles sculpt capacitor holes in one tool
idea: Combine spatial (rotary-platen) atomic layer deposition with atomic layer etching on one platen. Alternating sectors deposit a protective liner at the hole top and quasi-isotropically etch the bowed and tapered zones, reshaping each high-aspect-ratio hole into a straight cylinder in one pass.
why: Replaces separate etch-deposit-etch profile-correction loops across 3-4 tools. Straight walls give ~20% more Cs at the same AR (fact 1) and ~15% fewer chamber-hours.

title: Heat-vanishing polymer capacitor mold eliminates the support lattice
idea: Combine BEOL air-gap sacrificial polymers (thermally decomposable polycarbonate/polynorbornene) with the capacitor mold. Holes are etched in the polymer and low-temperature PEALD electrodes are formed, then the mold is removed by dry burnout rather than an HF wet strip, so no capillary forces topple the pillars.
why: Wet-strip capillary leaning is why 1-3 SiN support lattices are needed. Dropping them removes ~2 masks and ~12 steps and allows AR beyond 75 (facts 1, 4).

title: Array buried-channel transistor reused as the only periphery transistor
idea: Combine the array's recessed-channel buried-wordline transistor with periphery logic: decoders, sense control and I/O are built only from the same BCAT-style devices (upsized, paralleled, dynamic logic styles), and the separate HKMG planar periphery module is deleted.
why: The HKMG periphery module adds ~8-12 masks plus integration complexity. Deleting it removes ~10-15% of mask count and periphery-specific tools, and more bank parallelism absorbs the speed cost.

title: Vacuum-linked cluster runs the whole capacitor module airlessly
idea: Combine the cluster-tool concept with the full capacitor module (mold deposition, HAR etch, dry mold removal, electrode ALD, high-k ALD, top plate) on one vacuum transfer backbone. Wafers never see air, wet cleans or FOUP queues inside the module.
why: Removes ~5 wet cleans and their tools, eliminates native-oxide and queue-time losses, and shrinks the module's cleanroom footprint ~40% (capital intensity, water use).

title: LNG-style take-or-pay project finance for DRAM fabs
idea: Combine the LNG-terminal project-finance structure, where 20-year take-or-pay offtake contracts serve as collateral, with DRAM fabs. Hyperscalers pre-buy fixed-price bit capacity, federal loan guarantees cover construction, and the fab SPV borrows at infrastructure rates instead of memory-cycle equity.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost (fact 4). Cutting WACC from ~12% to ~6% and stretching depreciation lowers wafer cost ~15-20% and de-risks U.S. builds.

title: NAND-grade LDPC replaces DRAM redundancy, fuses and laser repair
idea: Combine NAND flash's quasi-cyclic LDPC engine with DRAM. A rate-0.85 code in the base/buffer die absorbs a 1% raw cell BER, with a ~10 ns fast path for clean lines, so the DRAM die ships with no spare rows or columns, no fuse bank, no laser-repair pass and no repair-analysis test step.
why: Redundancy and fuses take ~5-8% of die area, and laser repair plus repair test take ~5% of back-end capex; together ~10% lower cost/bit (facts 4, 7).

title: Quarter-dose EUV exposures quadruple scanner throughput, stochastics absorbed
idea: Combine EUV exposure with error-tolerant cells: the contact and capacitor-hole layers are exposed at ~15 mJ/cm2 instead of ~60, and the resulting photon-shot-noise missing or merged features (~0.1-1% of cells) are accepted as cell errors handled by the code layer.
why: EUV throughput is dose-limited, so ~3-4x more wafers per scanner-hour cuts EUV cost per layer ~60% and the number of scarce single-supplier scanners needed (fact 4).

title: Bit-significance-aware arrays: dense sloppy LSB mats, robust MSB mats
idea: Combine the numeric structure of AI tensors with DRAM layout. One mask set prints two mat types: LSB mats at a near-failure tight pitch running ~1% BER, and sign/exponent/MSB mats at relaxed pitch. The controller swizzles each word so low-significance mantissa bits land in the dense mats.
why: About half the bits in BF16/FP8 tensors are low mantissa bits, so putting them in ~25% denser mats gives ~10-15% more bits per wafer with no new node (density, cost/bit).

title: Erasure-coded HBM stacks built from barely tested dies
idea: Combine storage-array Reed-Solomon erasure coding with HBM stacking: 12+2 dies are stacked with only a gross-short screen, and each line is striped across dies with RS(14,12). Up to two dead dies plus 1% cell errors per die are tolerated.
why: HBM stack yield is down 20-30% and pre-stack known-good-die test is costly (fact 6). Erasure coding raises stack yield toward ~99% and removes most pre-stack test.

title: Delete retention-tail implants and anneals; codes absorb the leakers
idea: Combine the cell recipe with system coding: the halo and compensation implant masks and the extended hydrogen anneal, which exist only to tame the 13 fA leakage tail, are removed. The ~1% of cells that then fall below 64 ms retention are absorbed by scrub plus code.
why: Drops ~2-3 implant masks and a long furnace step (~3% wafer cost) and the multi-hour hot retention-screen test (fact 3).

title: Fat landing pads printed by immersion, bridged pairs tolerated
idea: Combine enlarged storage-node landing pads with bridge-aware interleaving: overlay can drift +/-4 nm instead of +/-2 nm, and the ~1% of pads that short to a neighbor create paired errors that the code interleave is built to absorb. A 193i scanner can then replace EUV on that layer.
why: Overlay, not resolution, drives EUV on the landing-pad layer. Moving one EUV layer to immersion saves ~$100-150 per wafer and scarce EUV hours (fact 4).

title: Interleaved product codes let array layers run in ISO-5 bays
idea: Combine particle-defect statistics with 2D-interleaved product codes in which each codeword spans cells at least 1 um apart in both axes, and with segmented wordlines and bitlines, so a killer particle costs one symbol per codeword. Less critical array back-end layers then run in ISO-5 bays rather than ISO-3 minienvironments.
why: Cleanroom build is ~15-20% of fab capex and HVAC is a major energy draw; a relaxed class cuts that slice ~30% (capital intensity, energy).

title: Half-height capacitors: 2.5 fF cells sensed with code-assisted margin
idea: Combine a 30:1 capacitor mold, half today's height, with an offset-cancelling sense amp and the 1% error budget. Cs halves to ~2.5 fF, and the weakest ~1% of cells that mis-sense are left to the code.
why: Halves HAR etch time on the costliest tool fleet, removes one or two support lattices and reduces mold collapse; ~8-10% wafer cost and ~2x etch throughput (facts 1, 4).

title: Short-purge high-k ALD triples throughput, thin-bottom leakers tolerated
idea: Combine aggressive ALD cycle compression (3x shorter precursor exposure and purge in the capacitor ZrO2/Al2O3 stack) with error tolerance. The resulting thin or under-dense dielectric at the bottoms of some deep holes creates ~0.5% leaky cells that the code absorbs.
why: High-k ALD in AR 60-75 holes is slow and needs large tool fleets; 3x throughput cuts that fleet by two-thirds and saves precursor (capital intensity, throughput; fact 1).

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM routes around dead mats and bits
idea: Combine Cerebras-style wafer-scale integration with DRAM: the wafer is never diced but hybrid-bonded whole to a wafer-scale compute or interposer wafer. Mat-level crossbar routing disables dead mats, and a code layer covers 1% cell BER.
why: Removes dicing, per-die packaging, KGD sorting and the HBM TSV/microbump tax, giving ~2-3x bandwidth per edge-mm and ~20% back-end cost avoided (facts 5, 6).

title: Sketch-grade DRAM standard turns yield fallout into supply
idea: Combine yield-fallout bins with workloads that natively tolerate 1% bit errors (Bloom filters, count-min sketches, embedding tables, quantized KV-cache). A JEDEC-style approximate grade with an SPD flag and OS allocator lets these dies ship rather than be scrapped, with public research clusters as anchor buyers.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer started ~5-10% immediately at zero capex (supply strategy, capital intensity).

title: Atmospheric mist-CVD oxide channels for error-tolerant gain cells
idea: Combine atmospheric ultrasonic mist-CVD, as used for Ga2O3 and solar TCOs, with 2T gain cells: the In-Ga-Zn-O-like channel is deposited without vacuum sputtering or ALD, and ~1% of cells with off-current outliers are absorbed by the code layer.
why: Vacuum tools cost $3-8M each, while mist-CVD tools are ~10x cheaper with higher throughput, cutting BEOL memory-tier capex (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Beamlet-failure-tolerant multi-beam direct write for array layers
idea: Combine massively parallel e-beam writers with cell-level error tolerance: ~1% of beamlets may be dead or drifting with no per-beam correction or redundant rescan. The wafer shifts by a sub-pitch offset each pass so a dead beamlet scatters into isolated bad cells rather than whole lines.
why: Per-beamlet reliability and redundant rescans are what keep direct write too slow; relaxing them could raise throughput ~2-3x and make reticle-free, EUV-free array patterning plausible.

title: Cell-pitch hybrid bonding of separate capacitor and transistor wafers
idea: Combine wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding with the 1T1C cell: all capacitors are made on one wafer (free to use high thermal budget and high-k) and all access transistors on another. The wafers are bonded at ~40-60 nm pitch, and ~1% void-killed bonds are accepted as cell errors.
why: Each wafer flow sheds the other's constraints (~20% fewer steps, no capacitor-over-transistor thermal compromise), and the 1% budget makes sub-100 nm bonding yield-viable years earlier (facts 1, 2).

title: Colloidal nanosphere lattice patterns transistors and capacitors in register
idea: Combine nanosphere lithography with a vertical-channel 4F2 cell. A monolayer of ~25 nm beads, guided by coarse immersion-printed trenches so rows stay straight, defines the pillar transistors, and the same lattice, shrunk by etch, defines the capacitors above. The ~1% bead vacancies and dislocations are simply bad cells.
why: Removes 3-5 critical array masks and all array overlay steps, so array patterning capex collapses to coaters plus one coarse layer (fact 4).

title: Vertical codewords across tiers break 3D DRAM yield compounding
idea: Combine 3D NAND-style tier stacking with tier-orthogonal coding: each codeword takes one symbol from each of ~32 tiers along the vertical bitline, so a defective tier (lateral-transistor shorts, capacitor voids) costs only one symbol per codeword. Per-tier yield can then be 99% rather than 99.99%.
why: Tier-yield compounding is a hidden blocker for 26+ tiers (fact 2). Relaxed per-tier yield permits faster deposition, fewer inspections and ~2x more tiers per stack.

title: Burn-in deleted; field scrubbing absorbs infant-mortality bits
idea: Combine the patrol-scrub engine with infant-mortality physics: DRAM ships without 125 C multi-hour burn-in, because early-life weak bits (well under 1% of cells) surface as correctable errors that the scrubber remaps in the first weeks of service.
why: Burn-in ovens, boards and floor space are a notable share of test capex and cycle time; removing them cuts back-end cost ~3-5% and cycle time 1-2 days.

title: Sort-time error syndromes replace most inline metrology
idea: Combine code-layer syndrome counters with advanced process control: every probed die reports spatial maps of corrected bits, which are decoded into virtual metrology (CD, overlay, etch depth inferred from error signatures). Inline CD-SEM/OCD sampling can then drop ~70%.
why: Metrology and inspection are ~10-12% of fab capex. The 1% budget makes the slower feedback loop acceptable (capital intensity, throughput).

title: Masks with printable defects accepted as fixed erasure addresses
idea: Combine reticle defect maps with on-die bad-cell tables. A printable mask defect repeats at the same array address in every die, so masks with tens of array-region defects can skip repair and actinic re-inspection, and those addresses are preloaded as known erasures in every die's code layer.
why: EUV blanks, defect repair and actinic inspection are a chokepoint at $1M+ per mask, and known erasures cost half the code budget of random errors (fact 4).

title: Lower-grade crystals from recycled-quartz crucibles, leakers absorbed by codes
idea: Combine cheaper crystal growth (crucibles with thin synthetic liners over recycled or non-Spruce-Pine quartz, several pulls per crucible) with error tolerance. Higher oxygen-precipitate and metal densities lengthen the leakage tail, and the extra retention-weak cells are absorbed within the 1% budget.
why: Breaks the >80% Spruce Pine high-purity quartz chokepoint and cuts wafer cost ~20-30% (scarce resource).

title: Two-bit-per-capacitor DRAM made viable by 1% sensing tolerance
idea: Combine NAND's multi-level-cell sensing with the DRAM capacitor: four charge levels per cell are read by a charge-sharing, two-step successive-approximation sense amp. The scheme historically failed on margin but works once the code absorbs ~1% level misreads.
why: 2x bits per wafer with the same masks, litho and capacitor, roughly halving capital per bit (facts 1, 4).

title: Refurbished dry-ArF and KrF fleets run wider-tolerance array layers
idea: Combine the abundant used-tool market (refurbished dry ArF, KrF and older etchers) with cell-level error tolerance. Non-critical and semi-critical layers go to tools with ~2x worse CD uniformity and chamber matching, and the added variability (~0.1-0.5% bit errors) fits the 1% budget.
why: Used tools cost 10-30% of new, so a greenfield U.S. fab could cut capex ~20% and ramp sooner by sourcing tools immediately (capital, time, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Double-rate capacitor etch accepting rare not-open holes
idea: Combine high-power, high-rate HAR etch recipes with error tolerance: capacitor-hole etch rate is pushed ~2x with higher bias and fewer passivation cycles, and the resulting ~0.5-1% not-open or twisted holes become dead cells logged as erasures at sort.
why: HAR capacitor etch chambers are among the largest DRAM capex items, and 2x rate halves the fleet, worth $1B+ in a large fab (facts 1, 4).
